title: 3D CAD Architecture & Subassembly Breakdown
text:
Each component on this page is a solid model generated from the system’s design parameters, not drawn by hand. Its dimensions come from the physics-based sizing (loads, stresses, fatigue, vibration and thermal limits), and the browser shows the result as an interactive 3D model.
A boundary representation (B-rep) describes a solid by the surfaces that enclose it. It stores the faces (pieces of planes, cylinders, cones, tori or NURBS surfaces), the edges where faces meet and the vertices where edges meet, together with the topology that records which face borders which [1–3]. Because the boundary is exact, a bearing bore is a true cylinder of a known diameter, and volume, mass, centre of gravity and moments of inertia follow directly from the geometry. A B-rep model is parametric when every dimension is an expression of named inputs, such as auger diameter, flight pitch, bearing size or mast section, instead of a fixed number [4]. When a derivation changes a value (for example the flute depth set by the fatigue check), the solids rebuild with the new value and every dependent dimension follows.
An application programming interface (API) is the set of functions that one piece of software publishes so that other programs can use it. WebGL is such an interface: a JavaScript API, standardised by the Khronos Group, through which a web page sends triangles, material colours and lights to the computer’s graphics processor (GPU) [5]. The viewers on this page use it to draw each model at interactive frame rates in any modern browser, with no plug-in.
The models are published in three file formats, each suited to a different task:

title: 3D CAD Architecture & Subassembly Breakdown
text:
1 Modelling approach
Every part is modelled once as a parametric B-rep solid by the CAD generator, sized from the same parameter set and design derivations used in the sizing calculations. The same solids are written to colour-labelled, assembly-structured STEP files (mm), tessellated to STL (mm), and tessellated to glTF .glb (m, Y-up) for the viewers below. The web models and the engineering STEP files therefore always match.
Tessellation. The STEP file keeps the exact curved surfaces, but a GPU or a 3D printer can only process flat triangles. Tessellation replaces each curved face by a mesh of triangles whose vertices lie on the true surface, so each triangle edge is a chord across the curve. The error is the chordal deviation, the largest gap between a triangle and the surface it replaces. For a face of radius r divided into segments that each span an angle \theta:

\delta = r\left(1 - \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\right)



\delta: chordal deviation, the largest distance between the true surface and the triangle that replaces it (mm)
r: local radius of curvature of the face (mm)
\theta: angle one segment spans at the centre of curvature (rad)


The generator holds \delta \le 0.08 mm and \theta \le 0.25 rad. On the 10 mm radius of the auger flight, the deviation limit alone would allow \theta = 0.253 rad, so the angular limit governs and a full circle becomes 26 segments. The worst-case error is 0.8 % of the radius, below what a screen can show and below ordinary machining tolerances. Thin, repeated features (helical flights, bristle tufts, coil springs) use coarser limits to keep the files small. The web copy is also converted to the glTF convention of metres with +Y up [8]: a CAD point (x, y, z) in millimetres with Z up becomes (x,\ z,\ -y)\times10^{-3} m. That is a rotation of -90^\circ about the x-axis followed by a scale, so the frame stays right-handed and lengths, angles and the hand of every helix are preserved.
Home pose. The rig is drawn at 1:1 scale in its home pose, the reference configuration from which every motion is measured. In robot-kinematics terms it is the zero position of the prismatic feed joint [9]. The carriage sits at the top of its travel on the rails, so the drill string is fully withdrawn and the bit tip hangs 300 mm above the regolith. That height clears the mast foot plate (100 mm) and the top of the brush (about 223 mm), so the parked bit touches neither the brushing station nor the ground and the load cell reads no weight on bit. To reach the 1.0 m target depth the carriage therefore needs a stroke of 0.30 + 1.00 = 1.30 m. A mission starts and ends here: the controller leaves home, approaches at 5 mm/s until the load cell detects 5 N of contact, and returns to home after the last bite. The digital twin moves the carriage by the displacement \Delta z = z_\text{tip} - z_\text{home} from this pose.


\Delta z: carriage displacement from the home pose, positive upward (m)
z_\text{tip}: bit-tip height above the regolith surface at the current instant, negative once the bit is in the hole (m)
z_\text{home}: bit-tip height in the home pose, 0.30 m


Colour code. The colours carry engineering meaning. Each part is coloured by the job it does in the machine, so a load or energy path can be traced by eye, as in the cutaway drawings of engineering manuals. Finishes are matte, in the manner of technical illustration, so that hue rather than mirror-like highlights carries the information [10]. The eight function hues are the Okabe–Ito colour-universal-design set, chosen so the classes stay distinguishable for readers with colour-vision deficiency, about one man in twelve [11, 12]. Two neutral greys mark the primary structure and the lander. The same colours are written into the STEP part labels, so the code carries into any CAD package.

Gears, spindle, shafts, bearings, leadscrew, nut and rails that transmit torque and feed force

Avionics warm box, radiator and H2/O2 reactant tanks

Deck section, legs and footpads that the drill reacts against



Primary structure
Housings, mast spine, plates, brackets, frames and clamps that carry the loads




Read together, the classes follow the energy through the machine: electrical power is converted in the motors (blue), carried as torque and feed force through the drive train (orange) or stored and released as impact in the percussion path (vermillion), delivered to the rock by the carbide (black), and the reactions return to the lander through the structure (greys). A part’s class follows its role, not its material: the bronze leadscrew nut is orange because it transmits feed force, while the bronze chute is green because it carries the sample.
In every viewer below, drag to orbit, scroll to zoom and right-drag to pan. The tag under each title gives the part count and the overall envelope (width × depth × height). The Download menu offers each model in the three file formats.

Cutters: two WC-10Co chisel inserts, -10° rake / 15° clearance (wedge 85°), edges on the line through the axis so the centre is cut, 2 mm proud of the face. Edge radius 1.00 mm from Hertz contact: carbide FOS 2.08 on a basalt clast, yet 36× the strength of the hardest ice.Junk slots: two 8 mm slots ahead of each rake face, sized so their area equals the sampling-flute channel (never the bottleneck). 1.2 Dual-zone auger string

Flights: 20 mm OD over the full length. The upper transport flight runs on a 14/12 mm hollow tube at 39.0 mm pitch (36.1° helix, the screw-efficiency optimum 45° − φ/2).Flight attachment: the root carries the stall plug pressure (3.5 MPa, 65 MPa bending) plus an inertial load at every blow's stress-wave front (136 MPa, 3.7e+07 cycles). Fillet welds are strong enough statically, but the weld toe would last only 2.0e+05 cycles (IIW FAT 63), so the flight is machined integral with the tube with a root fillet of t/2: Goodman FOS 2.21.String dynamics: a beam model of the 1240 mm string (sampling root, joint, tube, hex) gives a first lateral mode of 46 Hz at the start of the hole (1.77× the blow rate). Without the mast-foot guide bushing (22 mm Vespel liner) it would be 19 Hz, inside the ±20 % resonance band. Buckling 3,294 N vs a 167 N lift-off WOB; first torsional mode 393 Hz; wind-up 13.2° at 6.5 N·m, mostly in the 6 mm sampling root.Drive interface: a 16 mm hex sits 52 mm deep in the anvil socket (flank pressure 3.5 MPa, torsion 13 MPa, impact 47 MPa at the pin section). The tube is brazed into the collar (3 mm lap, FOS 19) and its end bears on the socket floor, so the blow never loads the braze. A cross pin (35 MPa at the load-cell rating) carries the hanging string.Thermocouple path: a 1 mm type-T lead runs from the bit probe through a spring-loaded coaxial contact at the bit joint (so the bit screws on without twisting it), up the tube and the chamfered hex bore to the slip ring; it fills 6 % of the narrowest bore.

Rotary drive: frameless BLDC sized from the 6.5 N·m spindle limit: 0.46 N·m at the rotor gives a Ø31 mm rotor in a Ø54 mm stator. It drives an 8:1 planetary (12/36/84 teeth, 3 planets, module 0.5) and a 12T/24T spur stage (module 1.25). Bending stress is 123 MPa and contact stress 923 MPa, both within AGMA limits for carburised 9310.Percussion: a second BLDC drives a 54T ring gear on a two-lobe barrel cam. The cycloidal rise lasts 150°, followed by a 30° dwell, twice the 2.7 ms the hammer takes to fall. The pressure angle peaks at 8.7° and roller contact stress at 528 MPa. The spring is the thinnest stock wire that passes every check: 6.0 mm wire, 3.14 active coils, 360 MPa, fatigue FOS 1.55, surge 682 Hz.Load paths: the hammer and anvil both slide on a DIN 5480 spline (flank pressure 4.6 MPa). The 5.4 kN blow travels from hammer to anvil to hex shank and never crosses a bearing. Weight on bit takes a different route: nut, yoke, a 500 N load cell (error 1.2 N, well under the 5 N contact threshold), the housing, the 7004 ACD pair, and the spindle end face. The Tr16×4 screw is self-locking.Bearings (SKF catalogue): 7004 ACD pair L10 = 104,061 h, 61804 35,847 h, 61812 cam bearing 18,528 h. The requirement is 400 h, 4× the drilling time. Dust: labyrinth and PTFE lip seal at the spindle exit, a stationary bellows over the 4 mm anvil float, and rail wipers on the LM16UU bushings.Quarter section: the housing and the coaxial stack are cut away in one quadrant. From the bottom up: anvil with hex socket, hammer with follower rollers on the barrel cam, spring, 7004 bearing pair, slip ring, 61804 bearing, 24T gear, then the planetary and motor in the offset pod, the load cell and the yoke.

Architecture: the drill rides on the fore edge of a 0.6 × 1.5 m lander deck section. It launches folded aft over the deck; a strain-wave hinge actuator swings it 90° to vertical, where spring latch pins on two deck posts lock it 250 mm above the hinge. Sequence: SMA hold-down release → carriage to home → deploy → latch → release the brush arm.Spine: 80×80×3 mm 6061-T6 Al box, the lightest of 240 (material, section, bracket count, latch height) combinations that passes every check (64 pass the deployed ones). Deployed first mode 20.0–21.2 Hz over the drilling stroke: between the cam (13 Hz) and blow (26 Hz) bands with ≥20% separation, 2% from the nearest band edge. Spine 5.4 kg, rotating assembly 24.9 kg incl. 20% growth allowance. The spine is in tension while drilling; buckling matters only when pulling a stuck string (FOS 218).Rails & alignment: 4 brackets support the Ø16 rails every 357 mm; their necks pass the slot of open LM16UU-OP bushings. An end-supported rail would be a 10 Hz string at launch. Under the 167 N lift-off WOB plus a 619 N single-cutter side load, spine bending, slope and rail flex move the string 0.49 mm off the guide-bushing axis (clearance 0.5 mm): a 3.7 mm bit alignment error at 1 m.Leadscrew: buckling 2,005 N on the compression side (FOS 12); whirl critical speed 558 rpm, with retraction at 34% of it (limit 80 %). The self-locking Tr16×4 nut holds the carriage at launch (3.5 MPa).Hinge, latch & actuator: Ø6 mm 17-4PH pins in double shear at a 14.5 kN launch lug load (FOS 2.4). Deploying needs 53 N·m against Mars gravity with the mast horizontal. ECSS motorisation (2× gravity, friction and harness + 1.25× inertia) gives 108 N·m, a Ø48 mm rotor through a 100:1 strain-wave gear. Earth tests need a g-offload. The latch is sized by stiffness (647 N per pin).Lander tilt: a side-mounted drill pushes up 0.35 m from the lander CG, so the near legs unload at 0.82 m g, before the lander lifts. The set-point stays m g / 1.4. The far legs sit 1.94 m behind the drill so the tilt limit (60 N Moon, 137 N Mars) stays above the set-point plus the load-cell error. The tilt margin is 1.15, against 1.4 for a drill through the CG. Footpad friction alone reacts the torque limit (FOS 2.4 on the Moon), so no regolith anchors are needed.Stow pose: the carriage parks 701 mm below home, chosen to maximise the weakest local mode. The nut then splits the leadscrew (22 Hz) and the guide bushing props the string (23 Hz); left at home both would be ~10 Hz. At 15 g (GEVS Miles 3σ) the screw sees 124 MPa and the string 200 MPa.Stowed primary mode: 97 Hz on the hinge plus 2 hold-downs (requirement 50 Hz; a single hold-down at the crosshead would give 45 Hz with this spine). Launch loads are the larger of 15 g quasi-static and the Miles 3σ response; spine stress 47 MPa (yield FOS 5.1).Hold-downs: pyro-free SMA-released A-286 M8 frangible bolts in cup-cone pedestals. They carry 6.6 kN at launch, and the preload keeps the joint closed with NASA-STD-5020 separation and ultimate factors. The cones carry shear, the hinge carries load along the mast, and the actuator gearbox carries none.


1.5 Brushing station and sample carousel

  
    
      Brushing station, exploded60 parts · envelope 210 × 239 × 255 mm
      DownloadSTEPexact B-rep, assembly tree, mmSTLtriangle mesh, mmglTF binary (.glb)web mesh with materials, m

Brush as a worm wheel: the sampling flight is a single-start worm, and the 14 bristle tufts are the wheel teeth on a 29.0 mm pitch radius (35.5 mm from the auger axis), leaning 17.7° at the flight lead. The tuft count is the smallest that enters and leaves the flute without touching a flight and still leaves a 1 mm hub ligament. The brush turns one tuft per auger revolution. The 39 mm transport pitch is exactly 3× the sampling pitch, so the transport flight meshes too.Bristles: 0.10 mm 17-7PH wire, tips 0.2 mm past the flute root. Their tip pressure is 59 kPa, 13× the cuttings' Rankine passive pressure, at 72 MPa (Goodman FOS 12.8). Thicker wire would wear longer, but with the bit above the guide bushing the string is a 1.24 m cantilever. The total contact force (0.36 N) must stay under the 0.44 N that would push the bit past the bushing lead-in.Drag & mission: derived drag 2.9 mN·m with full flutes (plough + bristle friction + bushings), 0.67 mN·m on empty flights. Both feed the state machine. The root-contact patch sets the sweep speed to 2.6 mm/s (87 s per bite).Spring-loaded arm: two 55 mm arms hang from pivot pins below the axle, so the line-of-centres force acts at 90° to them and the arm load does not depend on gravity. The arm floats on the bristles: a 0.8 mm torsion spring, wound up 14°, preloads it with exactly the required bristle force (0.36 N). When the bit crown's gauge step passes, the force rises only 3.7 %. The axle runs in Vespel SP-3 bushings (PV 9 Pa·m/s, far below the limit).Chute & cup: one bite gives 52 cm³ of bulked cuttings. The bronze chute is pitched at 32°, 10° steeper than the cuttings-on-bronze friction angle, and its inlet wraps the auger at the bit's largest re-entry excursion. The lunar flow layer is only 0.2 mm deep. A bronze funnel carries the stream through a port in the mast foot plate into that bite's cup.Sample carousel: each bite gets its own cup. The 10 cups (Ø37.8 mm × 55.5 mm, 120 % of one bite) hang on a turntable under the foot plate, on a 82 mm pitch radius with one blank station (11 stations). The cups are as deep as the ground clearance allows, which keeps the bore and the carousel small. The plate is their lid: PTFE face seals on every rim bear on its underside, and only the cup under the port is open. A stepper with a planetary gearhead on the plate indexes one station in 6 s while the auger descends for the next bite, so indexing adds no mission time. With every cup full, ECSS motorisation needs 0.31 N·m, most of it seal drag, against 0.70 N·m rated, at 0.07 W. The carousel adds 0.82 kg to the mast foot, which the mast frequency, hold-down and deployment sizing above already include.Planetary protection: the arm swings 13° to a stowed position that a launch lock holds through launch and the pre-flight dry-heat bake-out, with the tips clear of the bit. Every brush-station material (17-4PH, 17-7PH, phosphor bronze, Vespel, Ti) tolerates the bake-out temperature. Open risk: a thin layer of cohesive fines may still cling to the chute in lunar gravity. Every cup except the one being filled stays sealed, and the blank station keeps all ten sealed through launch, bake-out and after the last bite, which limits cross-contamination between samples.

2 Integrated drill rig and kinematic structure

  
    
      Complete drill rig, home pose286 parts · envelope 3593 × 2249 × 2222 mm
      DownloadSTEPexact B-rep, assembly tree, mmSTLtriangle mesh, mmglTF binary (.glb)web mesh with materials, m
    
    
      Model failed to load. Serve the site over HTTP; browsers block .glb files opened directly from disk.
    
  
The complete assembly brings every subassembly above onto the lander at its true position. It is stored as a scene graph: a tree of nodes, each holding a coordinate frame (a position and an orientation relative to its parent node) and the parts attached to that frame [13]. A node inherits every motion of its parent and adds its own. A part’s pose in the world is therefore the product of the transforms along the path from the root of the tree to the node that holds it:

\mathbf{T}_\text{world} = \mathbf{T}_1\,\mathbf{T}_2 \cdots \mathbf{T}_n



\mathbf{T}_\text{world}: 4\times4 homogeneous transform giving the part’s position (m) and orientation in the world frame
\mathbf{T}_1 \ldots \mathbf{T}_n: transform of each node relative to its parent, from the root (1) down to the node that holds the part (n); each combines a 3\times3 rotation and a translation (m)


This is the forward-kinematics rule used for serial robot arms [9]. The tree follows the physical joints of the machine: parts that are bolted together share one node, because a rigid body has a single pose, and a new node starts wherever a joint lets one group move relative to another. The solar wings show the nesting most clearly. Each elevation node is the child of an azimuth node, which is the child of the static power-system node, so turning a turntable carries the yoke and panels round with it, and the elevation tilt is then applied in the turned frame, exactly as in a two-axis gimbal. The drill-head nodes (carriage, auger, hammer, cam) sit side by side under the root and receive the same feed displacement, which is equivalent to a rigid attachment to the carriage. With this structure, one number per joint is enough to pose the whole machine.
The numbers come from state-machine telemetry. The drill’s autonomy software is a finite-state machine: at every instant it is in exactly one of six states (IDLE, ACTIVE, SEARCH, DRILL, RETRACTION, TRANSFER) and it moves to another only when a defined physical condition is met [14]. For example, SEARCH becomes DRILL when the load cell reads the contact force, and DRILL becomes RETRACTION when the bite reaches its length or when a temperature or torque limit trips. The mission simulation steps this machine forward once per second, solving the cutting mechanics, the bit’s heat balance and the sun geometry at each step. It records the result as telemetry, a time series of 29 columns that include bit-tip depth, weight on bit, spindle speed and torque, percussion duty, bit temperature, sun azimuth and elevation, and carousel station. The digital twin on the Results & Digital Twin page [15] reads this record and turns each channel into a joint coordinate: depth sets the carriage translation, spindle speed is integrated over time into the auger’s spin angle, the sun angles set the wing gimbals and the bite counter sets the carousel index. The animation is therefore a replay of what the simulated controller did, not a scripted sequence.

The table lists each node of the scene graph: how many parts it carries, what they are, and the motion the digital twin gives it. Two nodes are static. The frame node (lander deck, legs, hinge, latch and the deployed, latched mast) and the power-system base carry loads but do not move while drilling. Counting the remaining joints gives the mobility of the machine. Eight coordinates are independent, each driven by its own actuator: the carriage feed (a prismatic joint, leadscrew motor), the spindle rotation (rotary motor), the barrel-cam rotation (percussion motor), the carousel index (stepper) and the azimuth and elevation of both solar wings (four gimbal motors). The other motions are dependent, fixed by kinematic constraints rather than by motors. The auger, hammer and cam translate with the carriage. The hammer turns with the spindle through its spline and rises and drops as a function of the cam angle. The brush has no motor at all: it is a worm wheel meshing with the auger flight, so its speed follows from the flight lead and the motion of the string,

\omega_b = \frac{1}{r_p}\left(\frac{\omega_a\,p}{2\pi} + v_z\right)



\omega_b: angular speed of the brush (rad/s)
r_p: pitch radius of the brush tufts, 29.0 mm
\omega_a: angular speed of the auger (rad/s)
p: lead of the flight passing the brush, 13.0 mm in the sampling zone and 39.0 mm in the transport zone
v_z: axial speed of the string past the brush (m/s)


This split between independent and dependent motions is why the controller needs only eight commanded set-points to pose a 286-part machine. The barrel cam’s spin is drawn at a reduced rate so it stays readable. The hammer stroke is drawn at the true blow rate of 26 Hz, which a 60 Hz display can only just resolve: about 2.3 frames per blow, against the minimum of two samples per cycle set by the sampling theorem [16].

title: 6-State Autonomous Control & Mission Telemetry
text:
A drilling mission is a set of quantities that change continuously in time: the depth of the bit, the torque on the auger, the temperature of the bit and the electrical power drawn. Each one obeys a physical law written as a rate of change, for example “the bit warms at a rate set by the heat flowing in minus the heat flowing out”. A computer cannot follow a continuous change exactly, so the mission is advanced in small, equal time steps. This is called a discrete-time or time-stepping simulation [1]. In this model the step is \Delta t = 1 s, which is why the simulation is described as second-by-second. At each step the controller reads the simulated sensors, chooses its commands, and every state variable is moved forward by one step:
x_{k+1} = x_k + \Delta t \, f(x_k, u_k)
This update is the explicit (forward) Euler method [1]. It is accurate when \Delta t is much shorter than the fastest physical process being followed. The fastest process here is the bit cooling into dense ice, with a thermal time constant of about 57 s from a lumped heat balance [2], so a 1 s step resolves it with an error of a few per cent. The fastest drilling rate is 5 mm/s, so the bit moves at most 5 mm per step. Individual hammer blows (26 per second) are faster than the step and are not followed one by one; their average energy per second enters the cutting law instead [3]. The result is a full mission record, 3462 time steps on the Moon and 2725 on Mars, produced by the same physics that sizes the hardware on the other pages. A model of this kind, which runs the hardware’s own physics and control logic forward in time, is the core of a digital twin [4]. Nothing in the record is scripted: faults appear only when a physical quantity crosses a limit.

text:
1 The 6-state algorithm





stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> IDLE
  IDLE --> ACTIVE: 20 s health check done
  ACTIVE --> SEARCH: actuators >= 213 K
  SEARCH --> DRILL: load cell >= 5 N (bottom found)
  DRILL --> RETRACTION: bite complete (10 cm)
  DRILL --> RETRACTION: torque >= 5.53 N·m (fault)
  DRILL --> RETRACTION: T_bit >= T_crit (fault)
  RETRACTION --> SEARCH: thermal fault, bit cooled in hole
  RETRACTION --> TRANSFER: flutes at brushing station (or cooling > 30 min)
  TRANSFER --> SEARCH: next bite, or resume bite after torque fault
  TRANSFER --> IDLE: 1.0 m reached, stow






The controller is a finite-state machine: at any moment it is in exactly one of six states, and each state has its own control law. It moves to another state only when a measured quantity meets a condition, called a guard, written on each arrow above. Statecharts of this kind are a standard way to specify reactive control software [5]. Because each state also drives continuous physics (depth, torque, temperature), the full system is a hybrid automaton, a machine with discrete modes and continuous dynamics inside each mode [6, 7]. The guards use only quantities a real drill can measure: a load cell for contact with the hole bottom, motor current for torque, a temperature sensor near the bit and the feed position for depth. The sequence SEARCH → DRILL → RETRACTION → TRANSFER is one “bite”: the drill cuts 10 cm, pulls the auger out with the cuttings held in its flutes, and brushes them into a sample cup. The Icebreaker Mars drill and the TRIDENT lunar drill use the same bite cycle, so that each sample comes from a known depth interval and the hole cools between bites [8, 9]. Detecting faults from torque and temperature and recovering without an operator follows the approach demonstrated in Arctic field tests of autonomous planetary drills [10]. The diagram was checked against the simulation code: every arrow corresponds to a branch in the code, and the thresholds on the arrows are the values the simulation uses.




State
Control law (as simulated)




IDLE
20 s avionics / sensor check; stow to home at the end.


ACTIVE
95 W heaters until the actuators reach 213 K (lubricant limit + 20 K): 18.9 min Moon, 3.6 min Mars (lumped heat balance).


SEARCH
Descend at 12.5 mm/s until 2 cm above the last hole bottom, then 5 mm/s until the load cell reads 5 N.


DRILL
Hold WOB at m g / 1.4. Each step, evaluate rotary-only and rotary-percussive and pick the lower specific energy. Derate RPM linearly over the last 30 K before Tcrit.


RETRACTION
Bite done or torque fault: trip out without rotation, so the cuttings stay in the flutes. Thermal fault: lift 3 cm off the bottom and wait until Tbit < Tcrit − 15 K.


TRANSFER
Rotate at 65 rpm while sweeping the 225 mm sampling zone past the brush at 2.61 mm/s (87 s).




The units and symbols in the table are:


s (second) and min (minute): time, used for durations such as the 20 s health check and the warm-up time
W (watt): power, the rate of energy use; the heaters draw 95 W, i.e. 95 J every second
K (kelvin): absolute temperature, where 0 K is absolute zero and 273.15 K is 0 °C; 213 K is −60 °C. A temperature difference in kelvin, such as the 30 K derating band or the 15 K margin, is the same size as one in °C
mm/s (millimetres per second): speed of the bit along the hole, for the feed during SEARCH and for the brush sweep during TRANSFER
cm and mm (centimetres, millimetres): lengths, such as the 2 cm approach clearance, the 3 cm lift after a thermal fault and the 225 mm sampling zone
N (newton): force, as read by the load cell; 5 N is roughly the weight of a 0.5 kg mass on Earth
WOB (weight on bit): the downward force pressing the bit into the ground (N)
m g / 1.4: the WOB set-point, where m = 45 kg is the mass of the lander that reacts the drilling force, g is the local gravity (1.62 m/s² Moon, 3.71 m/s² Mars [11, 12]) and 1.4 is a safety factor that keeps 40 % margin against lifting the lander. This gives 52 N on the Moon and 119 N on Mars
rpm or RPM (revolutions per minute): rotational speed of the auger; 65 rpm is just over one turn per second
T_{bit}: temperature of the bit (K)
T_{crit}: the highest bit temperature allowed before ice in the ground would sublimate (Moon) or melt (Mars), 163.5 K on the Moon and 263.15 K on Mars

title: 6-State Autonomous Control & Mission Telemetry
text:
2 Nominal mission telemetry
                                                
The four panels share one time axis, so an event in one can be traced through the others.
Bit depth. The solid line is the bit tip and the dotted line is the bottom of the hole. Each tooth of the saw pattern is one bite: the bit descends to the hole bottom, cuts 10 cm, then rises above the surface (negative depth) to the brushing station and returns. The hole bottom therefore climbs in ten steps to 100 cm. The slope of the solid line while it moves down with the hole bottom is the rate of penetration (ROP). It reaches the 5 mm/s feed limit in loose, dry soil and falls as low as 1.2 mm/s in ice-cemented ground, whose compressive strength is 5–22 MPa against a few kPa for dry soil [13, 14]. Stronger ground takes more energy to break per unit volume, so with the same power the hole advances more slowly [15]. The long flat stretches between cuts are trips in and out of the hole, which is why the bite cycle, not the cutting, sets the mission length [8].
Auger torque. Torque is the twisting load the rotary motor must supply. On a drag bit it has two parts: the force needed to shear the ground ahead of the cutters, and friction on the worn cutter edges pressed down by the WOB [16]. Retained cuttings rubbing on the hole wall add a third part. In the nominal mission the torque stays between 0.11 and 0.49 N·m, far below the 5.53 N·m fault threshold, because the WOB is small in low gravity and each 10 cm bite fits inside the flutes. Mars torque is higher because the WOB is 2.3 times larger (stronger gravity) and the ice-rich layers are thicker. In each step the controller also decides whether to switch on the hammer. It computes the mechanical specific energy (MSE), the energy spent per unit volume of hole, for rotary-only and for rotary-percussive cutting and keeps whichever is lower [15, 17]. Percussion was chosen for 27 % of drilling time on the Moon and 71 % on Mars, almost entirely in the hard, ice-cemented layers where hammer blows chip the brittle ground more cheaply than scraping [18].
Bit temperature. Cutting turns mechanical work into heat at the bit face, and about a quarter of it flows into the bit [19]. The bit loses heat by conduction into the surrounding ground and by the fresh cuttings carrying heat away; outside the hole it radiates to the sky. The simulation treats the bit as a single lumped mass, whose temperature changes at a rate equal to heat in minus heat out divided by its heat capacity [2]. The bit warms during each cut and cools on every trip, so the trace rises and falls with the bites. The peak is 120 K on the Moon (from 100 K ground) and 205 K on Mars (from 192 K). The dashed lines are the limits T_{crit}. On the Moon the limit is set by sublimation: above about 164 K the vapour pressure of ice rises steeply and the sample would lose its water before analysis [20, 21]. On Mars the limit is 10 K below the melting point of ice. Laboratory drilling under Martian conditions showed that ice melted by a warm bit refreezes on it and can trap the drill [22]. Both stay well clear, with 43 K of margin on the Moon and 58 K on Mars, so the thermal derating and the thermal fault path are never triggered.
Electrical load and solar supply. The solid line is the power drawn: avionics, plus heaters during warm-up, plus the rotary, hammer and feed motors during drilling. It peaks at 130 W. The dotted line is the output of the two-axis tracking solar array. At the lunar south pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon and has no atmosphere to cross, so a tracking array delivers a steady 857 W over the hour-long mission [23, 24]. Mars is 1.52 times farther from the Sun, so sunlight at the top of its atmosphere is only about 43 % as strong (inverse-square law), and suspended dust (optical depth 0.45) absorbs and scatters more of it [12, 25]. The Mars array therefore gives 241–254 W, varying slowly with the Sun’s height. Supply exceeds load at every step on both bodies, so the battery stays full and is never discharged.
                                                
Only 13 % (Moon) and 23 % (Mars) of the mission is spent cutting rock. Tripping in and out ten times and warming the actuators dominate. That is the real cost of bite-drilling, and the reason Icebreaker-class drills take about an hour per metre [8].
Time in each state. The bar chart adds up the seconds spent in each state. ACTIVE (actuator warm-up) takes 18.9 min on the Moon but only 3.6 min on Mars. The lunar ground starts at 100 K against 192 K on Mars, so the heaters must lift the actuators by 113 K instead of 21 K to reach 213 K, the lowest temperature at which their lubricant works with a 20 K margin. SEARCH, RETRACTION and TRANSFER are identical on both bodies because they are set by feed speeds and the brushing sweep, not by the ground. TRANSFER is the largest of these at 87 s per bite: the brush must sweep the full sampling zone slowly enough to strip every flute. DRILL is longer on Mars (10.3 min against 7.3 min) because more of its column is hard ice-cemented ground. Shortening the mission would mean longer bites (fewer trips), which the next section shows is limited by flute capacity.

title: 6-State Autonomous Control & Mission Telemetry
text:
3 Fault recovery
Nominal mission: 0 faults. With 10 cm bites inside the 12.25 cm flute capacity,
the auger never chokes. The bit also peaks at 120 K (Moon) and 205 K (Mars), well below
the 164 K and 263 K limits. Nothing is scripted, so the fault paths stay quiet.

3.1 Flute capacity and choking onset
The lower part of the auger is the sampling zone: a section with deep, closely spaced flutes (the helical grooves between the flights) that holds the cuttings of one bite while the auger is pulled out. Broken ground takes up more room than intact ground, because the grains no longer pack tightly; the ratio of loose to intact volume is the bulking factor [26]. The flutes are therefore full once the bit has cut a certain length of hole. That length is the choking onset depth z_{crit}:

z_{crit} = \frac{L_s \, A_{flute}}{A_{hole} \, B}



z_{crit}: choking onset, the length of hole that can be cut in one bite before the sampling flutes are completely full (m)
L_s: length of the sampling zone (m); here 225 mm
A_{flute}: open cross-section of the flutes available for cuttings (m²); here 282.9 mm²
A_{hole}: cross-section of the hole (m²); here 346.4 mm². Cutting a length z of hole removes a volume A_{hole} z of intact ground
B: bulking factor, the volume of loose cuttings divided by the volume of intact ground they came from, 1.5 (dimensionless; 1.3–1.6 for granular regolith [26])


The numerator is the volume the flutes can hold, and the denominator is the loose volume of cuttings produced per metre of hole. Their ratio gives z_{crit} = 0.1225 m, or 12.2 cm. The sampling zone was sized to hold 120 % of one 10 cm bite, so a nominal bite fills the flutes to 82 % and leaves margin.
Choking onset is the moment cuttings have nowhere left to go in the sampling zone. Beyond z_{crit}, newly cut material is forced up into the narrower transport flutes above and packs into a plug. A plug of granular material in a tube behaves like grain in a silo: part of the push is turned sideways into pressure on the walls, and wall friction resists the motion. Janssen showed that this friction makes the force needed to move the plug grow exponentially with its length [27, 28]:

\sigma_{plug} = \sigma_0 \exp\!\left(\frac{4 \mu_w K L_{plug}}{D_h}\right), \qquad L_{plug} = \frac{(z_{bite} - z_{crit}) \, A_{hole} \, B}{A_{transport}}



\sigma_{plug}: pressure the auger flights must apply to push the plug along (Pa)
\sigma_0: strength of the loose cuttings at the start of the plug, from their cohesion and friction angle (Pa)
\mu_w: friction coefficient between cuttings and the hole wall, 0.42 (dimensionless)
K: ratio of sideways to axial pressure in the plug, 1 - \sin\phi with \phi the friction angle of the cuttings [29] (dimensionless)
L_{plug}: length of the compacted plug (m)
D_h: hydraulic diameter of the transport flute channel, four times its area divided by its perimeter (m)
z_{bite}: length of hole cut so far in the current bite (m)
A_{transport}: open cross-section of the transport flutes (m²)


The auger must turn against this pressure, so the motor torque rises gently up to z_{crit} and then steeply beyond it. The chart below evaluates the model at 90 cm depth for bites of increasing length. This sudden torque rise, ending in a stalled auger, is the failure that field and laboratory tests of planetary augers call choking [18, 30]; screw-conveyor theory gives the same picture of throughput collapsing once the flights are overfilled [31].
                                                


3.2 Off-nominal case: 15 cm bites
To test the fault path, the same mission was simulated with 15 cm bites, longer than z_{crit} = 12.2 cm. Nothing else was changed and no fault was scripted. In each bite the torque stays low for the first 12.2 cm, then climbs as the plug forms. When it reaches 5.53 N·m (85 % of the motor’s 6.5 N·m limit, kept in reserve so the string is never twisted to its limit), the controller leaves DRILL. It stops rotation and pulls the auger out (RETRACTION), so the packed cuttings stay in the flutes rather than spilling back down the hole. It brushes them into the sample cup (TRANSFER), returns to the hole bottom (SEARCH) and finishes the bite with empty flutes. The table lists every fault the physics produced.

The torque column is the value in the step that crossed the threshold; it can overshoot well past 5.53 N·m because plug resistance grows exponentially and the controller acts once per second. In nearly pure ground ice on Mars the modelled torque jumps to over 18 N·m within a single step. A real motor would stall at its current limit before that, which is why the trip point sits below the limit and why flight software samples torque much faster than once per second. Choking trips the fault in 6 of 7 bites on Mars, where most of the column is dense ice-cemented ground, and in 3 of 7 bites on the Moon. Both missions still reach 1.0 m: the Moon in 49 min (58 min nominal) and Mars in 55 min (45 min nominal). The Moon finishes sooner because fewer, longer bites mean fewer trips; Mars takes longer because each choked bite needs an extra trip out and back. Longer bites are therefore possible, but every choke stresses the auger and mixes cuttings from a wider depth range into one cup, which is why the nominal design keeps each bite inside z_{crit}. Monitoring torque and retracting on overload is the same recovery used by autonomous drills tested in the field [8, 10].

title: Mission Results & Digital Twin
text:
The goal is to collect ice-bearing samples from 1 m below the surface at the lunar south pole and in Mars’s northern high latitudes. Water ice in the top metre has been detected at both sites: in the LCROSS impact plume at the lunar south pole [1] and directly under the Phoenix lander at 68° N on Mars [2, 3]. That ice is both a resource for future missions and a record of how volatiles reached and survived on these bodies. Each depth interval has to come up intact and correctly labelled. The ice must not be lost to the heat of drilling.
Four physical constraints make this difficult, and each one shaped the design:

Low gravity limits how hard the bit can be pushed. A small lander can only press the bit down with its own weight. Surface gravity is 1.62 m/s² on the Moon and 3.71 m/s² on Mars [4, 5], so a 45 kg lander weighs only 73 N on the Moon and 167 N on Mars. Pushing harder than that lifts the lander off the ground, and the drill runs with a safety margin below that limit. Laboratory tests on icy regolith show that its strength rises steeply with ice content and falling temperature, reaching about 5–20 MPa in compression at cryogenic temperatures [6]. Frozen Martian ground and ice at about 190 K fall in the same range [7]. In such material a rotary drag bit needs about 139 N before its cutters start to cut rather than rub [8]. So rotary drilling alone stalls. A cam-and-spring hammer solves this, as it did on the Icebreaker and TRIDENT prototypes [9, 10]: it delivers 2.25 J per blow, 26 times a second, breaking rock with impact energy instead of steady force [11].
There is no drilling fluid. In vacuum or a thin CO₂ atmosphere of about 6 mbar [5], cuttings cannot be flushed out with mud or air as they are on Earth, so an auger carries them [12, 13]. At a safe rotation speed, centrifugal friction is too weak to lift cuttings against gravity on either body. The drill therefore works in 10 cm “bites”, the approach Icebreaker uses [9]: it cuts, holds the cuttings in deep sampling flutes, pulls the auger out, and a passive brush strips them into a sample cup. The flutes are sized to hold one bite. Drilling further in one pass packs the cuttings into a plug whose wall friction grows exponentially with length, as Janssen’s silo analysis predicts [14], and the auger chokes.
Heat can destroy the sample. Friction warms the bit. Lunar polar cold traps sit below about 110 K [15], and ice in the cuttings sublimates into vacuum quickly once warmed. Using the measured vapour pressure of ice [16, 17], the model sets the bit limit at about 164 K on the Moon. On Mars, ice that melts and refreezes can freeze the bit into the hole, which Icebreaker field tests experienced [9]. The controller watches the bit temperature and backs off before either limit.
Sunlight arrives almost horizontally. At the lunar south pole the sun stays within about 1.5° of the horizon [18]. Flat panels collect almost nothing, so the solar wings stand near-vertical and track the sun [19]. On Mars they also tilt in elevation.

Modelling approach. The model starts from four kinds of input, each with a cited source: measured properties of the Moon and Mars (gravity, soil strength, temperature, sunlight), design choices (lander mass, bit size, bite length), published values from drilling and materials research, and safety factors from NASA and ECSS engineering standards [20, 21]. Every other figure on this site is calculated from those inputs with established engineering models: drag-bit cutting mechanics [8], impact stress waves [11], Goodman fatigue [22], Janssen granular friction [14], ice vapour pressure [16], sun geometry and heat balance. A second-by-second simulation then runs the whole 1 m mission. No value is adjusted to reach a target. The results are compared with the closest field-tested prototype, Honeybee Robotics’ Icebreaker drill [9], and the same models also generate the 3D CAD shown on this site.

title: Mission Results & Digital Twin
text:
The goal is to collect ice-bearing samples from 1 m below the surface at the lunar south pole and in Mars’s northern high latitudes. Water ice in the top metre has been detected at both sites: in the LCROSS impact plume at the lunar south pole [1] and directly under the Phoenix lander at 68° N on Mars [2, 3]. That ice is both a resource for future missions and a record of how volatiles reached and survived on these bodies. Each depth interval has to come up intact and correctly labelled. The ice must not be lost to the heat of drilling.
Four physical constraints make this difficult, and each one shaped the design:

Low gravity limits how hard the bit can be pushed. A small lander can only press the bit down with its own weight. Surface gravity is 1.62 m/s² on the Moon and 3.71 m/s² on Mars [4, 5], so a 45 kg lander weighs only 73 N on the Moon and 167 N on Mars. Pushing harder than that lifts the lander off the ground, and the drill runs with a safety margin below that limit. Laboratory tests on icy regolith show that its strength rises steeply with ice content and falling temperature, reaching about 5–20 MPa in compression at cryogenic temperatures [6]. Frozen Martian ground and ice at about 190 K fall in the same range [7]. In such material a rotary drag bit needs about 139 N before its cutters start to cut rather than rub [8]. So rotary drilling alone stalls. A cam-and-spring hammer solves this, as it did on the Icebreaker and TRIDENT prototypes [9, 10]: it delivers 2.25 J per blow, 26 times a second, breaking rock with impact energy instead of steady force [11].
There is no drilling fluid. In vacuum or a thin CO₂ atmosphere of about 6 mbar [5], cuttings cannot be flushed out with mud or air as they are on Earth, so an auger carries them [12, 13]. At a safe rotation speed, centrifugal friction is too weak to lift cuttings against gravity on either body. The drill therefore works in 10 cm “bites”, the approach Icebreaker uses [9]: it cuts, holds the cuttings in deep sampling flutes, pulls the auger out, and a passive brush strips them into a sample cup. The flutes are sized to hold one bite. Drilling further in one pass packs the cuttings into a plug whose wall friction grows exponentially with length, as Janssen’s silo analysis predicts [14], and the auger chokes.
Heat can destroy the sample. Friction warms the bit. Lunar polar cold traps sit below about 110 K [15], and ice in the cuttings sublimates into vacuum quickly once warmed. Using the measured vapour pressure of ice [16, 17], the model sets the bit limit at about 164 K on the Moon. On Mars, ice that melts and refreezes can freeze the bit into the hole, which Icebreaker field tests experienced [9]. The controller watches the bit temperature and backs off before either limit.
Sunlight arrives almost horizontally. At the lunar south pole the sun stays within about 1.5° of the horizon [18]. Flat panels collect almost nothing, so the solar wings stand near-vertical and track the sun [19]. On Mars they also tilt in elevation.

Modelling approach. The model starts from four kinds of input, each with a cited source: measured properties of the Moon and Mars (gravity, soil strength, temperature, sunlight), design choices (lander mass, bit size, bite length), published values from drilling and materials research, and safety factors from NASA and ECSS engineering standards [20, 21]. Every other figure on this site is calculated from those inputs with established engineering models: drag-bit cutting mechanics [8], impact stress waves [11], Goodman fatigue [22], Janssen granular friction [14], ice vapour pressure [16], sun geometry and heat balance. A second-by-second simulation then runs the whole 1 m mission. No value is adjusted to reach a target. The results are compared with the closest field-tested prototype, Honeybee Robotics’ Icebreaker drill [9], and the same models also generate the 3D CAD shown on this site.

2 Bit design compared with oilfield practice
An oilfield PDC (polycrystalline diamond compact) bit has a wide body with many blades of diamond cutters, nozzles for drilling mud and a threaded pin [23, 24]. Extraterrestrial drills, such as Honeybee Robotics’ Icebreaker and the TRIDENT drill built for NASA’s PRIME-1 and VIPER missions, use a small carbide-tipped bit on the end of an auger instead [9, 10]. The conditions are too different for the oilfield design to work:

Oilfield PDC bits after the IADC fixed-cutter classification and Bellin et al. [23, 24]; extraterrestrial bit practice after Zacny et al. [9, 12].

Three physical reasons rule the PDC design out:

Heat. Without mud to cool them, diamond cutters overheat. The diamond layer degrades above roughly 700 °C, because the cobalt binder expands faster than the diamond, and frictional heating in dry or poorly cooled drilling can reach that at the cutting edge [25].
Impact. Diamond is brittle and chips under hammer blows. Cemented carbide is tough enough to take 26 blows per second, which is why percussion bits in mining use carbide inserts [13, 26].
Load per cutter. A cutter only bites when it carries enough force. A few tens of newtons shared across dozens of cutters gives almost nothing per cutter, so a low-gravity bit concentrates its load on two edges [8].

Some oilfield practice does carry over. The bit uses negative back-rake (-10°), as PDC cutters do to resist chipping [23]. It also has gauge pads to hold the hole size and junk slots between the cutters to clear cuttings.

The four cards summarise what the simulation returns for each body. Each value comes out of the model; none is an input.
What goes into the model.

Ground column. Each site is described as a stack of layers with a compressive strength (UCS) for each. The lunar column runs from loose dry regolith [27] to icy regolith of about 5 and 20 MPa [6]. The Martian column follows the Phoenix site: ice-cemented ground from a few centimetres down, over nearly pure ice [2, 3, 7].
Lander and drill. A 45 kg lander, a 21 mm bit with two carbide cutters, a 10 cm bite, a 150 RPM nominal auger speed and a 5 mm/s feed-rate ceiling.
Safety criteria. A safety factor on lander lift-off, a temperature limit on the bit and a torque limit on the auger string.

How the model turns those inputs into the cards.

Weight on bit (card C). Weight on bit (WOB) is the downward force pressing the bit into the ground. The lander can only supply its own weight, m g: 73 N on the Moon and 167 N on Mars. Pushing harder lifts the lander. The controller’s set-point, the force it is told to hold, is that weight divided by a factor of safety (FOS) of 1.4: WOBset = m g / FOS. This gives 52 N on the Moon and 119 N on Mars, so the drill never uses more than about 71 % of the lander’s weight. The value 1.4 is the ultimate-load factor NASA-STD-5001B applies to tested spaceflight structures [20]. A load cell under the drill head closes the loop around this set-point.
Cutting mode and penetration rate. At each depth the model compares the set-point with the force a rotary drag bit needs before it cuts, from the Detournay–Defourny cutter model [8]. It then works out the penetration rate in both rotary and rotary-percussive mode, using specific energy (the energy needed to remove a unit volume of rock) [28, 29]. The controller picks whichever mode removes rock with less energy. The rate is capped at the 5 mm/s feed ceiling.
Power (card D). Drilling power is the sum of rotary power (torque × speed), hammer power, feed power and avionics, each divided by its motor and gearbox efficiency. Heaters add to the peak when the actuators are warmed before motion.
Time and depth (cards A and B). A state machine steps through the mission one second at a time: warm-up, search for the surface, drill one bite, retract, brush the cuttings into the cup, and repeat ten times. Bit temperature, battery charge and solar input are integrated on every step. The mission time is the sum of these phases. Pure drilling takes only 7.3 min on the Moon and 10.3 min on Mars. Most of the rest is retraction and sample transfer, plus 19 min of actuator warm-up on the colder Moon.

Comparison with a field-tested prototype. Honeybee Robotics’ Icebreaker drill is the closest working prototype. Its field tests reported a “1-1-100-100” result: about 1 m in about 1 hour, with under 100 N weight on bit and about 100 W [9]. This model predicts 0.76 h, 119 N and 105 W while drilling on Mars. These are the same order of magnitude as the prototype, and no coefficient was fitted to that benchmark. Model uncertainty is shown on the Derivations & Design page.

title: Mission Results & Digital Twin
text:
6 Bite-by-bite performance
                                                
The three panels show, for each 10 cm bite, the average penetration rate, the mean drilling power and the mechanical specific energy (MSE). MSE is the energy spent to remove one cubic metre of ground. Teale introduced it as a measure of drilling efficiency [28], and it is now used to monitor oilfield drilling in real time [30]. For an efficient cutter, MSE is close to the compressive strength of the rock [29, 31]. A rise in MSE therefore means harder ground or a less efficient cutting mode. It is plotted on a log scale because it spans almost two orders of magnitude.
Moon.

Bites 1–5 (dry regolith). Loose regolith has almost no strength [27]. The bit drills at the 5 mm/s feed ceiling with rotary cutting alone, and MSE is only about 1.1 MJ/m³. Each bite takes 20 s.
Bites 6–8 (icy regolith, about 5 MPa). The rotary threshold is now about 35 N, still below the 52 N set-point, so the bit keeps cutting in rotary mode. The rate falls to 1.4 mm/s.
Bites 9–10 (ice-rich regolith, about 20 MPa). The rotary threshold rises to about 139 N, well above the set-point, so rotary cutting would stall. The controller switches on the hammer. Power jumps to about 122 W and MSE to about 63 MJ/m³. Percussion is less efficient than clean rotary cutting, in line with field experience [11, 30], but it is the only way to make progress with the force available. The bit warms to 120 K, well below the 164 K sublimation limit.

Mars.

Bites 1–8 (ice-cemented ground, 18–22 MPa). At the Phoenix site, ice-cemented ground starts a few centimetres below the surface [3]. Even with Mars’s stronger gravity, the 119 N set-point is below the rotary threshold of about 125–152 N, so the hammer runs almost all the time. The rate is 1.9–1.5 mm/s at about 125 W.
Bites 9–10 (nearly pure ice, about 12 MPa). Ice at about 190 K is weaker than ice-cemented soil [7]. The rotary threshold drops to about 83 N, below the set-point, so rotary cutting becomes possible again. Rotary-percussive mode would actually be faster here, but rotary cutting removes the ice with about 19 MJ/m³ against roughly double that with the hammer. Because the controller chooses the lower-energy mode, power falls to about 54 W at a rate of 1.2 mm/s. The bit stays at or below 205 K, far from the melt margin.

What this shows. Across both bodies, percussion runs for 27 % of drilling time on the Moon and 71 % on Mars. Percussion is what lets a light lander drill hard frozen ground, as the Icebreaker and TRIDENT prototypes showed [9, 10]. Bite length, not drilling rate, sets most of the mission time: each 10 cm bite needs a full retract-and-brush cycle, which takes longer than the cutting itself.

title: Design Showcase: a Rotary-Percussive Bite Drill for the Moon and Mars
text:
The problem
Water ice in the top metre of the lunar south pole and of Mars’s northern plains is both a resource for future crews and a record of how volatiles got there. A science lander needs to bring it up in labelled depth intervals, without melting or sublimating the ice on the way. Terrestrial drilling relies on heavy rigs, tens of kN of weight on bit and drilling mud. None of that is available here.
This project designs the complete drill system, from the carbide cutter edge to the solar wings, for a 45 kg lander at two sites: the lunar south pole (sun ~1.5° above the horizon) and Mars at 68° N.

title: Design Showcase: a Rotary-Percussive Bite Drill for the Moon and Mars
text:
Four constraints that drive everything
Low gravity73 Nis all the lander can push on the Moon before it lifts off. Ice-cemented regolith needs more than that to start rotary cutting.No drilling fluid0.64lift ratio for cuttings on a spinning auger (Moon). Below 1, the flights cannot carry cuttings to the surface.Heat164 Kbit temperature above which ice in the cuttings sublimates into vacuum (Moon). On Mars the limit is melting, at 263 K.Low sun~1.5°sun elevation at the lunar south pole. Flat panels collect almost nothing, so the solar array has to stand up and track.
The lift-off limit is simply the lander’s weight in local gravity. The heat limit comes from the vapour pressure of ice [1]: above it, the ice in a 25 µm cuttings grain is lost to vacuum within one bite. At the lunar south pole the sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon [2, 3].
The design rule was no tuned numbers. A tuned number is a value picked or adjusted until the answer looks right: a fudge factor, a coefficient fitted to the result you want, or a size chosen by eye. None is used here. Every input carries one of four tags, each with its source:

Environment fact: gravity, temperature, regolith strength and density [4, 5].
Design choice: for example the 10 cm bite or the 150 rpm spindle speed, each with its stated reason.
Literature coefficient: for example a friction coefficient, taken from a published range.
Safety criterion: a factor of safety or margin from a standard [6].

Everything else (176 derived quantities in the design ledger) is calculated from well-known engineering models:

Teale’s mechanical specific energy and the Detournay–Defourny drag-bit model for rock cutting [7–9]
Lundberg’s one-dimensional stress-wave model for percussion [10]
Hertz contact theory for the cutter edge [11]
Goodman and Wahl fatigue checks for shafts and springs [12], and the IIW FAT classes for welds [13]
Cycloidal cam motion and the 30° pressure-angle limit [14]
AGMA gear contact stress and ISO 281 bearing life [15, 16]
Euler–Bernoulli beam modes and Euler buckling for the drill string and mast [12, 17]
Rankine earth pressure and Janssen silo pressure for packed cuttings [18, 19]
Hertz–Knudsen sublimation of ice [1]
ECSS motorisation factors and AIAA mass-growth allowances for the mechanisms [20, 21]

A second-by-second mission simulation then checks the whole design.

title: Design Showcase: a Rotary-Percussive Bite Drill for the Moon and Mars
text:
Key design decisions

1. The bit: two carbide chisels, not an oilfield PDC
Bit crown: two WC chisel inserts, gauge pads, junk slots and the sampling flutesExploded bit: inserts, crown body, gauge pads, thermocouple, sampling sub and M12x1 joint

Concentrated load. With only 52 N on the Moon, the load has to go into as few edges as possible. Two WC-10Co chisel inserts give a line load of 271 N/mm, enough to crush the hardest layer by a factor of 36. In drag-bit cutting models, a cutter only removes rock once its contact stress beats the rock strength [8, 9]. With so little weight available, spreading it over many cutters would leave each one below that threshold.
Edge sized by contact mechanics. The worst case is a blow landing on a basalt clast. A Hertz line-contact check sets the edge hone at R1.0 mm (FOS 2.1 on carbide). Carbide is very strong in compression but weak in tension. The −10° (negative) rake keeps the cutting edge in compression, the same reason oilfield PDC cutters are set at negative rake [22].
Indexing. The bit turns 35° between blows, so each blow lands on fresh rock 6.3 mm from the last crater. Hitting the same crater again only re-grinds crushed material, which wastes energy and raises the specific energy of drilling [7, 10].
Why not PDC. PDC cutters are made for continuous shearing with drilling fluid flowing over them. Their thin diamond layer chips under impact, and the cobalt binder degrades the diamond above about 750 °C if the cutter is not cooled [22]. Under 26 Hz hammering and with no fluid, solid WC-Co carbide is the safer choice. Percussive rock-drill bits use tungsten-carbide button inserts for the same reason [23].



2. The drill head: a cam-and-spring hammer around a hollow spindle
Drill head quarter section: BLDC motors, planetary, cam-and-spring hammer, anvil and spindleDerived, not chosen
Impact energy 2.25 J at 26 Hz; peak force 5.4 kN (1-D stress-wave model)
Hammer spring: 6 mm 17-7PH wire, fatigue FOS 1.55; spring rate puts the hammer at 91 Hz, above 2× the blow rate so it re-seats every cycle
Barrel cam: cycloidal rise, pressure angle 8.7° (limit 30°)
Rotary drive: frameless BLDC through a 12/36/84 planetary and a 12T/24T spur; spur contact stress 923 MPa on carburised 9310
Spindle bearing pair L10 104,061 h; WOB measured by a 500 N load cell
Head stack 321 mm, sealed by labyrinth, PTFE lip seals and bellows

Rotary cutting alone stalls in ice-cemented regolith at this weight on bit. The hammer solves this by breaking rock with impact energy instead of steady force. The bit only has to stay seated, which takes 44 N, below the Moon set-point. A two-lobe barrel cam lifts the hammer, then drops it off a cliff in the cam profile onto the anvil. The rotary train runs through the hollow spindle beside it. The controller turns percussion on only when the measured torque and penetration rate show that rotary cutting has stopped working.
Each item in the card above comes from a standard method:

Impact energy and force. The blow is modelled as a stress wave travelling through the hammer, anvil and bit [10]. Percussion is the established answer to low weight on bit in planetary drilling. Both Icebreaker and TRIDENT use rotary-percussive heads [24–26].
Hammer spring. It is sized with the Wahl stress factor and checked against Zimmerli fatigue data using the Goodman criterion [12]. The spring’s natural frequency must stay above twice the blow rate. Otherwise the hammer cannot settle back onto the cam before the next lift.
Barrel cam. A cycloidal rise has zero acceleration at both ends, so the follower sees no shock loads. The pressure angle is kept below the usual 30° limit so the follower does not jam [14].
Gears and bearings. The spur gear contact stress is checked against the AGMA allowable [15]. The spindle bearing life follows ISO 281 [16].
Margins. Structural factors of safety follow NASA-STD-5001 [6].



3. Auger + brushing station: drilling in bites
Exploded brushing station: worm-wheel brush, spring arm, chute and sample cupDeployed mast on the lander deck: rails, leadscrew and brushing station

Bite drilling. With no drilling fluid, the only way out of the hole for cuttings is up the auger flights. A cutting climbs the flight only if the friction from the borehole wall, which the spin presses it against (centrifugal force), is larger than its weight. In other words, the lift ratio \mu_w \omega^2 r / g must exceed 1. Rotation speed is what governs dry auger conveying [24]. At the 150 rpm spindle speed this ratio is only 0.64 on the Moon and 0.28 on Mars. Continuous conveying would need more than 188 rpm on the Moon and 284 rpm on Mars.
Spinning that fast is the wrong trade for this drill. The speed was set low (0.16 m/s at the gauge) to limit frictional heat at the bit, which has to stay below 164 K on the Moon or the ice sublimates out of the sample [1]. A faster spin would also open the index angle between hammer blows. Dry augers in lunar regolith also tend to bind: the Apollo 15 crew had great difficulty drilling past about 1 m [24].
The drill therefore works in bites, like Icebreaker and TRIDENT [25, 26]. It drills a short interval, pulls the whole string out, and brushes the cuttings into a cup. The deep sampling flutes hold the cuttings from one bite. They fill completely after 12.2 cm of penetration, so the bite is set at 10 cm. Each bite is a depth-labelled sample, and the auger never has to carry cuttings the full depth, so it cannot choke.
Flights machined integral. Welded flights fail IIW weld-toe fatigue under hammer-wave inertia (2e+05 cycles against a 3.7e+07 requirement). Under the IIW recommendations, a fillet-welded attachment falls in fatigue class FAT 63, which is far too weak for this load [13]. A flight machined from the same bar, with a root fillet, has no weld toe. It gives a Goodman factor of safety of 2.2 [12].
Guide bushing. Without it, the string’s first lateral mode falls to 19 Hz, inside the blow-rate band. With it, the mode is 46 Hz. A structure driven near its natural frequency resonates, so every mode is kept out of a ±20 % band around each forcing frequency [17].
Passive brush. The brush is a 14-tuft wheel that meshes with the flights like a worm wheel, so the retracting auger drives it with no extra motor. The 0.1 mm bristles push at 59 kPa, 13× the cuttings’ passive pressure. The cuttings’ resistance is taken as Rankine passive earth pressure [18], using lunar regolith cohesion [4]. A 32° chute then delivers the cuttings into a cup sized for 120 % of one bite. Each bite has its own cup: 10 sealed cups ride on an indexing carousel under the mast foot plate, so every depth interval is kept as a separate, sealed sample. The chute is steeper than the wall-friction angle, so dry cuttings slide in any gravity. Brushing cuttings off the auger into a sample cup is also how Icebreaker delivers its samples [25].



4. Deployable side-mounted mast
Launch configuration: mast folded aft over the deck on two hold-downsLaunch and deploy
Spine 80x80x3 6061-T6 Al, the lightest of 64 feasible designs out of 240 searched (material × section × brackets × latch height)
Stowed first mode 97 Hz against a 50 Hz launch requirement; M8 A-286 frangible bolts released by SMA actuators (low-shock, non-pyrotechnic)
Deployed first mode 20–21 Hz over the stroke, placed between the cam and blow-rate bands
Deploy actuator 108 N·m (ECSS motorisation factors) through a 100:1 strain-wave gear
Bit position error 3.7 mm at 1 m depth

A 1.9 m mast does not fit on the lander upright for launch. It folds aft over the deck on a hinge, with two hold-downs carrying the 15 g launch load, and swings up on the surface. Mounting it on the side keeps the borehole clear of the lander’s own footprint and exhaust-disturbed soil. The price is that the lander tilts before it lifts, which costs some WOB margin (see the limitations below).
The reasons behind the card above:

Launch stiffness. A stowed payload must have its first mode above the launcher’s minimum so that it does not couple with the launch-vehicle dynamics. Launch loads are taken as the larger of the quasi-static load and the Miles random-vibration estimate [27].
Hold-down release. A shape-memory-alloy (SMA) actuator breaks a notched frangible bolt in tension. It produces far less release shock than a pyrotechnic bolt, which matters for the drill head’s bearings and sensors, and it can be tested and reset on the ground [28]. The bolt preload is sized with standard joint equations [12].
Deployment. The deploy actuator is sized with the ECSS motorisation factors: twice the resistive torques (gravity, friction and harness) plus 1.25 times the inertial torque [20].
Mass. All masses carry a 20 % mass-growth allowance [21], and structural factors follow NASA-STD-5001 [6].
Deployed modes. These are kept between the rotary, cam and blow-rate bands, for the same resonance reason as the drill string [17].



5. Power: standing, tracking solar wings
                                                
All five array layouts were simulated against the real sun track at each site. The 2-axis tracking (azimuth + elevation) wings deliver 797 W on the Moon and 143 W on Mars (dust and the thin atmosphere included). That is at least twice the 73 W mission-mean load, so the battery never runs down during a mission. The array has to stand vertical and track because the polar sun moves around the horizon instead of rising overhead [2, 3]. Irradiance uses the measured solar constant [29]. On Mars, dust settling on the panels was measured by Pathfinder at about 0.3 % per day, and that loss is included [30].

title: Design Showcase: a Rotary-Percussive Bite Drill for the Moon and Mars

Honest limitations and next steps

The mast mode is close to a forcing band. The deployed mast’s first mode (20–21 Hz) sits only 2 % from the edge of the blow-rate band. The first changes to test are a stiffer spine or a small shift in the blow rate.
Side mounting costs stability. The lander tips about its far legs before it lifts. The tilt margin at the WOB set-point is 1.15, against 1.4 for a centred drill.
Mass. The rotating mast assembly weighs 25 kg, and the steel rails are the largest single item. Lighter rails or a composite spine are the obvious next trade.
Sample transfer is slow. Brushing takes 87 s per bite (16 min per mission). It is limited by the low bristle force a 1.2 m cantilevered string can take.
The models are uncalibrated. Rock-cutting specific energy and the heat partition come from literature ranges. The sweeps on the derivations page show their effect: Mars mission time ranges from 0.68 to 0.84 h. Drilling tests in a cryogenic vacuum chamber are the next step.

title: Terramechanics, Design Derivations & Power Sizing
text: Terramechanics is the mechanics of soil and granular ground under the loads applied by a machine: how the ground deforms, shears and fails when a wheel, blade or cutter is pressed into it [1]. For a drill, the ground is lunar or Martian regolith, which may be cemented by water ice. Its resistance to cutting is set by its cohesion, internal friction and ice content. Design derivations take that resistance and apply Newton’s laws, conservation of energy, stress-wave mechanics and fatigue theory to fix each dimension of the drill: the bit load, the hammer, the auger flutes. Power sizing closes the energy balance. The electrical energy the drill consumes must be supplied by the solar array, with the battery covering any shortfall, at the solar flux and gravity of each body.

title: Terramechanics, Design Derivations & Power Sizing
text:
1 Method
The model is built in three layers, so every result can be traced back to a stated assumption:

Primary inputs. Each value carries a tag:

[ENV]: an environment fact, with its source (gravity, temperature, ground strength).
[DES]: a design choice, with its rationale.
[COEF]: an empirical coefficient from the literature, with its plausible range.
[CRIT]: an acceptance criterion or a factor of safety.

Derivations turn those inputs into sizes and limits. All of them are listed in the derivation table at the bottom of this page.
Simulation integrates the drilling mission second by second with those sizes. No factor is adjusted afterwards to reach a desired result.

An acceptance criterion is a physical limit that a computed quantity must satisfy for the design to be accepted. Examples are a bit temperature below the point where ice is lost, or a bit load below the load that would lift the lander. A factor of safety (FOS) is the ratio of the capacity of a part to the demand placed on it:
FOS = \frac{\text{capacity}}{\text{demand}} \;\; \left(\text{e.g. } \frac{S_y}{\sigma} \text{ for strength}\right)
where


S_y: yield strength of the material, the stress at which it starts to deform permanently (Pa)
\sigma: largest stress the part carries in service (Pa)


A design with FOS > 1 can carry its load. The margin above 1 covers uncertainty in the loads, the material properties and the model itself. Spaceflight structures use factors of 1.25–1.4 on ultimate strength [2]. Parts under repeated load, such as the auger under hammer blows, are checked against fatigue strength instead [3].

UCS (unconfined, or uniaxial, compressive strength), \sigma_c, is the axial stress at which a sample of the ground fails when it is compressed along one axis with no side support. It is measured in pascals (1 kPa = 10³ Pa, 1 MPa = 10⁶ Pa) and sets how hard the ground is to cut. Dry regolith fails at a few kPa. Ice-cemented ground fails at tens of MPa, about four orders of magnitude higher. Thermal conductivity, k, is the rate of heat flow through a 1 m thick layer of 1 m² area per kelvin of temperature difference across it. Its unit is the watt per metre-kelvin, written W/(m·K) or W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. It controls how fast the drill bit can shed its frictional heat into the ground. Ice content is the mass of water ice per unit mass of the ground, in weight percent.
The dry layers have no ice to bind the grains, so their strength comes only from cohesion and friction. Their UCS follows from the Mohr–Coulomb failure criterion under uniaxial load [4, 5]:
\sigma_c = 2c\tan\!\left(45^\circ + \frac{\phi}{2}\right)
where


\sigma_c: unconfined compressive strength (Pa)
c: cohesion, the shear strength of the ground at zero normal stress (Pa)
\phi: angle of internal friction, which sets how shear strength grows with normal stress (°)


Cohesion and friction angle come from [6] (Moon) and [7] (Mars). The icy-layer strengths follow published trends for ice-cemented regolith [8, 9]. Thermal conductivities come from [6] and from the Phoenix probe measurements [10]. The Moon site is an ice-stable area near the Shackleton rim with a subsurface temperature of about 100 K [11]. The Mars site is the Phoenix landing area at 68°N, where the ice table sits about 5 cm down [12, 13].
These are representative values for each site. Every design parameter below is a function of these ground properties (\sigma_c, \phi, c, k and ice content). If a site is characterised more closely, the same equations return new sizes. No one has drilled to 1 m at either site, so the properties are inferred in stages. Each stage uses a physical signal that reaches below the surface:

Neutron spectroscopy from orbit. Cosmic rays knock neutrons out of the top metre of ground. Hydrogen nuclei have nearly the same mass as a neutron, so they slow neutrons far more efficiently than heavier nuclei do. A drop in the epithermal neutron flux therefore marks hydrogen, most likely water ice, in the upper ~1 m. This mapped polar hydrogen on the Moon [14] and the ice-rich layer below a dry cover at high Martian latitudes [15].
Thermal infrared radiometry. Measured surface temperatures, together with a heat-conduction model, give the depth below which ice is stable against sublimation. This is how the cold traps near the lunar south pole were identified [11].
Reflectance spectra and impacts. Water ice absorbs near-infrared light at known wavelengths, which revealed exposed ice in shadowed lunar craters [16]. The LCROSS impactor threw up ejecta from a shadowed crater, and the water was measured directly in the plume [17]. On Mars, steep eroding scarps expose buried ice sheets in cross-section to high-resolution cameras [18].
In-situ contact. Landers measure strength directly. Apollo core tubes and penetrometers gave lunar density and cohesion [6]. Phoenix’s scoop found hard ice-cemented ground a few centimetres down [7, 13]. The InSight heat-flow probe stalled at about 40 cm in unexpectedly cohesive soil, which shows how far orbital estimates can be from the true ground [19].
The drill as a sensor. While drilling, the measured torque, bit load and penetration rate give the energy spent per unit volume of rock removed. That energy tracks the ground’s compressive strength [20]. The drill therefore measures UCS layer by layer as it advances, as the Icebreaker field tests showed [21].

3 Weight-on-bit limit
Weight on bit (WOB) is the axial force pressing the bit into the ground. The drill pushes against the lander, so the lander’s weight is the only reaction force available. The bit load must stay below the load that would lift the lander, with a margin:
WOB_{\lim} = m g, \qquad WOB_{set} = \frac{m g}{FOS}, \quad FOS = 1.4
where


WOB_{\lim}: lift-off limit, the bit load that would just lift the lander off the ground (N)
WOB_{set}: set-point, the bit load the feed controller holds while drilling (N)
m: deployed lander mass reacting the bit load, 45 kg
g: surface gravity, 1.62 m/s² (Moon) and 3.71 m/s² (Mars)
FOS: factor of safety on lift-off (dimensionless)


The factor of 1.4 follows NASA-STD-5001 practice for ultimate loads [2].

text:
4 Rotary cutting and its stall in icy ground under lunar gravity
The model is the drag-bit law of [22]. Rounded cutter edges behave as wear-flats of total length \ell, carrying a load W_f = \sigma\,\ell\,a before any cutting happens:
\delta = \frac{W - W_f}{\zeta\, a\, \varepsilon}\;(\le \text{cutter protrusion}), \quad T = \tfrac12 a^2\varepsilon\delta + \tfrac12\mu a W_f, \quad ROP_{rot} = \delta\,\frac{N}{60}
where


\delta: depth of cut per revolution of the bit (m)
W: weight on bit, the applied axial load (N)
W_f: threshold load carried by the wear-flats in contact with the ground before the cutters bite (N)
\sigma: contact stress under the wear-flats (Pa)
\ell: total wear-flat length of all cutters (m)
a: bit radius (m)
\zeta: ratio of normal to tangential cutting force on a cutter (dimensionless)
\varepsilon: intrinsic specific energy, the energy needed to cut a unit volume of ground (J/m³ = Pa)
T: torque on the bit (N·m)
\mu: friction coefficient under the wear-flats (dimensionless)
ROP_{rot}: rate of penetration by rotary cutting alone (m/s)
N: rotary speed (rev/min)


The values used are \varepsilon \approx \sigma \approx \sigma_c [23], \zeta = 0.6, a = 10.5 mm and \ell = 0.66 mm. In the icy layers W_f reaches about 139 N, far above the lunar set-point of 52 N. The rotary depth of cut therefore drops to zero there, and percussion has to do the work.

5 Percussion: the cam-spring hammer
The two-lobe barrel cam compresses the spring by the cam lift h and then releases the hammer onto the anvil:
E = \tfrac12 k_s h^2, \quad v = \sqrt{2E/m_h}, \quad F = v\frac{Z_h Z_r}{Z_h + Z_r}\;(Z = \rho c A), \quad W_{\min} = m_h v (1+e) f
where


E: blow energy, the spring energy released per blow (J)
k_s: spring stiffness (N/m)
h: cam lift, the spring compression per blow (m)
v: hammer speed at impact (m/s)
m_h: hammer mass (kg)
F: peak impact force carried into the drill rod (N)
Z_h, Z_r: mechanical impedance of the hammer and of the rod (N·s/m)
\rho: material density (kg/m³)

A: cross-sectional area (m²)
W_{\min}: smallest bit load that keeps the bit seated against the rebound of each blow (N)

6.1 Choking beyond the flute capacity
Once a bite exceeds z_{crit}, the surplus cuttings are pushed up the narrow transport flute as a compacted plug. The plug’s resistance grows exponentially with its length (Janssen, as for a plug pushed up a tube) [26]:

where

\sigma_0: axial stress at the free end of the plug (Pa)
\mu_w: friction coefficient between the cuttings and the hole wall (dimensionless)
K: ratio of lateral to axial stress in the plug (dimensionless)
L: plug length (m)
